transcript.content: Hello, welcome. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

I’m here because... well, most days I wake up already feeling like this big, gray weight is just sitting right on my chest. It's like I'm already exhausted before my feet even hit the floor. And it's strange because I've been doing landscaping for, what, twenty years now? You'd think being outside in the sun all day would help. My buddy Mike, he works on the crew with me, he's always talking about how getting your hands in the dirt is good for the soul. He grows these massive tomatoes in his backyard, says it's his therapy. I tried growing tomatoes once, but the squirrels got to them before they even turned red. Little pests just take one bite and leave the rest to rot. Anyway, even when I’m out there with the crew, or... or even around my kids at home, I just can’t shake this low, hollow feeling. It's like I’m just going through the motions, you know? Just... existing.
Have you noticed that you don’t enjoy things as much as you used to, even activities that used to make you happy, like spending time with your kids or working on your landscaping projects?

Yeah, I guess so. It's just... everything feels kind of flat. Even with the kids. They're good kids, you know? My oldest, Sarah, she just started looking at colleges. Wants to go somewhere out of state, maybe study marine biology. She's always loved the ocean. We took a trip to the coast a few years back, and she spent the whole time just staring into tide pools. Found a starfish that was missing an arm. Did you know they can grow those back? Just regenerate a whole new limb. Seems crazy to me. I wish people could do that, just... fix whatever's broken and keep going. But yeah, even when we're all together, watching a movie or having dinner, I'm just sitting there. I see them smiling and laughing, and I know I should be feeling something, but it's just... nothing. Same with work. I used to like seeing a yard come together after a long day, but now it's just dirt and grass. Just another lawn to mow.
Do you feel down or low most of the day, nearly every day?

Yeah, pretty much. Like I was saying before, it's just... most days I wake up and that gray weight is already there, just sitting on me. It's heavy. Really heavy. Like those bags of mulch we haul around at work. We get these huge pallets delivered, mostly that dark brown cedar stuff. People love the cedar because it smells nice and keeps the bugs away, but man, it is a pain to move when it's wet. It rained for three days straight last week, just a miserable, cold drizzle, and all those bags soaked it right up. Mike tweaked his back trying to lift one off the truck. I told him he needs to lift with his knees, but he never listens. Stubborn guy. But yeah, that's what it feels like. Just this constant, heavy, low feeling, pretty much all day, every day. Even when I'm out with Mike and the crew, or sitting at home with the kids, it's just this hollow feeling inside. Like I'm just going through the motions of being alive.
Have you found yourself feeling worthless or guilty about things more often than not? Like maybe you're not doing enough for your kids or your work isn't good enough?

I don't really know if I feel worthless, exactly. I mean, I try to do right by the kids, you know? Pay the bills, keep a roof over our heads. It's not easy these days. Prices for everything are just going up. You go to the grocery store for a gallon of milk and a loaf of bread, and suddenly you're out twenty bucks. And gas... don't even get me started on gas. We drive these big F-250s for work, pulling trailers full of mowers and edgers, and filling the tank on one of those things is like taking out a small loan. My boss, Frank, he's been talking about raising our rates just to cover the fuel costs, but he's worried we'll lose clients to the bigger companies that can eat the cost. Frank's a good guy, though. He let me borrow his power washer last spring to do my driveway. It's amazing how much dirt gets blasted out of the concrete. You don't even realize how gray it is until you see the white underneath. But... yeah, I don't know about feeling guilty. I just feel tired.
Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or weight lately—like eating less than usual or losing weight without trying?

I don't really think so. I mean, I eat about the same, I guess. Usually I just stop at the Wawa on the way to the job site and grab a hoagie. They have those touch screens now for the sandwiches. You just poke the screen and it prints a little ticket. It's weird not actually talking to the person making your food. But I guess nobody really wants to talk much anyway. 

Last week I was in there and the screen was frozen, and this guy behind me just started sighing real loud, tapping his foot. Wearing these expensive-looking loafers. You can always tell a guy who doesn't work on his feet by his shoes. My work boots, I have to replace them every year. The soles just get completely eaten up by kicking shovels and walking on concrete all day. I buy the same Red Wings every time, though. They take a couple weeks to break in, give you terrible blisters on your heels, but after that, they're like slippers. Best boots you can buy. I tried a cheaper brand once from Walmart, and my arches were screaming by noon. Never again. 

But, uh... what were we talking about? Oh, eating. Yeah, no, I just eat my sandwich. My work pants still fit exactly the same, so I guess my weight hasn't really changed or anything.
Have you noticed that you're moving more slowly than usual, or that you just can't sit still and feel restless a lot of the time?

I haven't really noticed anything like that. I mean, my body always aches, so maybe I move a little slower when my knees are acting up, but that's just from the job. You spend twenty years bending over pulling weeds and wrestling with heavy equipment, your joints are gonna complain. 

Speaking of equipment, we just got this new riding mower, a zero-turn Toro. Thing is a beast. You can spin it on a dime, which is great for getting around all the fancy flower beds people put in the middle of their lawns. I don't get why people do that, honestly. It just makes cutting the grass ten times harder. You have to edge around every single rock and mulch ring. And the rich neighborhoods, they always want these perfect diagonal stripes in the grass, like it's a baseball outfield or something. It looks nice, sure, but you have to overlap your lines just right, and if you mess up one pass, the whole yard looks crooked. 

Frank usually makes Mike do the striping because Mike's got a better eye for it, but Mike's been complaining about his back again. I told him he needs to go to a chiropractor or something, but he won't spend the money. He'd rather spend it on his truck. He just put these massive off-road tires on it, the kind that hum real loud when you drive on the highway. I don't know why you need mud tires when you live in the suburbs, but whatever makes him happy, I guess. 

But yeah, restless or moving slow? No, I don't think so. Just the usual aches and pains.
Have you noticed that you have trouble concentrating on things lately, like following conversations or making decisions?

I don't really know if I have trouble concentrating. I mean, I guess I just do what I need to do. Like at work, you don't really have to think too hard, you just follow the routine. Start the mower, cut the grass, blow the clippings off the driveway. 

We use these backpack blowers, Echo brand, and let me tell you, they get heavy after a few hours. The straps dig right into your shoulders. Plus, they're so loud you have to wear ear protection or your ears will be ringing for three days. I usually wear those big earmuffs, but some of the younger guys just use little foam earplugs. I tried those once, but I could never get them to stay in my ears right. They always popped out when I started sweating. And man, do you sweat out there in July. It gets so humid, the air feels like soup. You drink a gallon of water and you don't even have to use the bathroom because you just sweat it all out. 

Frank brings a big cooler of Gatorade sometimes, the lemon-lime kind. That's the best flavor. The blue one just tastes like melted Popsicles. But the cooler he has is one of those old Igloo ones with the push-button spout, and the button always gets stuck, so it just drips all over the back of the truck. It makes everything sticky, and then the yellow jackets start swarming around it. You ever get stung by a yellow jacket? It's not like a regular bee, they don't lose their stinger. They just keep getting you over and over. Mike got stung right on the eyelid last summer, and his whole face swelled up like a balloon. Looked like he went a few rounds with Mike Tyson. We had to send him home. 

So... wait, what were you asking me? About following conversations? Yeah, I don't know, I guess I'm fine. Just, you know, normal.
Have you noticed a big drop in your energy level lately, like you get tired much more easily even doing simple things?

Yeah, I definitely get tired. It's like... by midmorning, my body feels like I've already put in a full day of work, you know? Even on a Sunday, when I actually get to sleep in and I'm not doing anything heavy, I still just drag through the simplest stuff. Like loading up the tools, checking the job plans for the week, or even just trying to make dinner at night. It's exhausting.

Speaking of dinner, I usually just do frozen meals now. Stouffer's mostly. The lasagna isn't bad, but the plastic film on top always tears when you try to peel it back halfway through cooking. You're supposed to vent it, right? But it just rips into tiny shreds, and then you burn your fingers trying to pull it off the hot tray. The microwave I have is older than dirt, too. The turntable thing inside stopped spinning like three years ago. So the food gets boiling hot on the edges and stays frozen solid right in the middle. You have to take it out, stir it up, put it back in. It's a whole process. 

I bought that microwave at a yard sale down the street. The guy was selling a bunch of tools, too, but they were all cheap brands. Ryobi and stuff. I mean, Ryobi is fine if you're just hanging a picture frame, but if you're doing real work, you need DeWalt or Milwaukee. Frank swears by Makita, but I don't know, their batteries never seem to hold a charge in the cold. We were doing a fall cleanup last November, and the battery on the leaf blower died after twenty minutes. We had to rake the rest of the yard by hand. 

Oak leaves are the worst. They don't break down like maple leaves do. They just sit there like leather, and when they get wet, they stick to the grass like glue. You have to really scrape at them with the rake. And the acorns... don't even get me started on the acorns. If you hit an acorn with the mower blade, it shoots out the side like a bullet. Broke a window on a client's garage once. Frank was furious. 

But, uh, what was the question? Oh, energy. Yeah, no, I just have zero energy lately. Everything feels like walking through mud.
Have you felt this way—like you're dragging through life and nothing brings you joy—for most of the time over the past two years?

Yeah, it's actually been longer than two years. More like... about three years and three months, I'd say. It all started when the new groundskeeping contract changed our schedule, and those longer days just completely took over my life. We went from a normal shift to working sunup to sundown, and they made us start using this new app on our phones to track our routes. 

You have to clock in on the app when you get to a property, right? But the GPS on it is garbage. Half the time you're standing right in front of the leasing office, and the phone says you're two miles down the highway. You just stand there tapping the screen like an idiot. Frank got so mad at it one morning he threw his phone into the bed of the truck and it hit the edge of a spade. Cracked the screen right down the middle. He had one of those heavy-duty cases on it, too, but it hit the metal just right. 

Those spades, man, we had to sharpen them ourselves because the new management wouldn't pay for new equipment. You ever try to cut a clean bed edge with a dull shovel? It just bounces off the dirt and jars your shoulders. You gotta take an angle grinder to the blade and put a real edge on it. I used to have a really nice bench grinder in my garage for stuff like that, but the motor burnt out last winter. Pretty sure a mouse got in there and chewed the wiring. Mice love chewing on wires for some reason. They got into my buddy's Honda a while back and did like two grand worth of damage to his electrical system. 

So... wait, what did you ask me? About how long it's been? But yeah, like I said, about three years and three months of just... feeling this way. Ever since that contract flipped.

Between the start of your low mood three years ago and now, have there been any periods lasting two months or more where you felt significantly better—like your old self again—before the sadness returned?

No, I don't think so. It's just been this same heavy feeling the whole time, it never really lifts. Two months is a long time, though. Like, two months is basically our entire winter plowing season around here. 

We usually switch the trucks over right after Thanksgiving. Take the mowers off the trailers, hook up the salt spreaders in the back, and mount these big Boss V-plows on the front of the F-250s. You gotta make sure the hydraulic fluid is topped off before it gets really cold, or the wings on the plow won't fold right. Frank got stuck in a Wendy's parking lot at three in the morning a couple years ago because a hydraulic hose blew and the plow was stuck in the down position. He couldn't move the truck an inch. Had to just sit there freezing his tail off until the tow truck came. 

And the salt... man, the rock salt just eats right through the metal on those trucks. You can wash them every single week, but after two seasons, the wheel wells are just completely rusted out. I actually tried using that Fluid Film spray underneath my own truck to stop the rust. You ever use that stuff? It works great, but it smells like sheep, literally, because it's made out of lanolin or something. My truck smelled like a petting zoo for weeks. You'd park in the sun and the whole cab would just reek of it. 

Anyway... wait, what were you asking? Two months of something? Oh, right, feeling better. Yeah, no. No breaks like that. Just the same dragging feeling, whether it's summer or winter.

We went from a normal shift to working sunup to sundown, and they made us start using this new app on our phones to track our routes. 

You have to clock in on the app when you get to a property, right? But the GPS on it is garbage. Half the time you're standing right in front of the leasing office, and the phone says you're two miles down the highway. You just stand there tapping the screen like an idiot. Frank got so mad at it one morning he threw his phone into the bed of the truck and it hit the edge of a spade. Cracked the screen right down the middle. He had one of those heavy-duty cases on it, too, but it hit the metal just right. 

Those spades, man, we had to sharpen them ourselves because the new management wouldn't pay for new equipment. You ever try to cut a clean bed edge with a dull shovel? It just bounces off the dirt and jars your shoulders. You gotta take an angle grinder to the blade and put a real edge on it. I used to have a really nice bench grinder in my garage for stuff like that, but the motor burnt out last winter. Pretty sure a mouse got in there and chewed the wiring. Mice love chewing on wires for some reason. They got into my buddy's Honda a while back and did like two grand worth of damage to his electrical system. 

So... wait, what did you ask me? About how long it's been? But yeah, like I said, about three years and three months of just... feeling this way. Ever since that contract flipped.

inference.note: The patient has reported a persistent low mood, anhedonia, fatigue, and a duration of symptoms exceeding three years. This rules out F32.9 (episode not specified) and F33.0 (mild recurrent depression), as the symptoms are more severe and long-standing. Further clarification is needed to distinguish between F33.1 (moderate) and F33.2 (severe) based on functional impairment and presence of neurovegetative symptoms.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has had recurrent episodes of depression separated by at least 2 months without depression, which would support a diagnosis of Recurrent Depressive Disorder (F33.1), or if the depression has been continuous without significant remission for at least 2 years, which would support Persistent Depressive Disorder (F33.2).
doctor.question: Between the start of your low mood three years ago and now, have there been any periods lasting two months or more where you felt significantly better—like your old self again—before the sadness returned?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about periods of remission (feeling better for two months or more) during the course of the depression, which is not covered by any specific item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I don't think so. It's just been this same heavy feeling the whole time, it never really lifts. Two months is a long time, though. Like, two months is basically our entire winter plowing season around here. 

We usually switch the trucks over right after Thanksgiving. Take the mowers off the trailers, hook up the salt spreaders in the back, and mount these big Boss V-plows on the front of the F-250s. You gotta make sure the hydraulic fluid is topped off before it gets really cold, or the wings on the plow won't fold right. Frank got stuck in a Wendy's parking lot at three in the morning a couple years ago because a hydraulic hose blew and the plow was stuck in the down position. He couldn't move the truck an inch. Had to just sit there freezing his tail off until the tow truck came. 

And the salt... man, the rock salt just eats right through the metal on those trucks. You can wash them every single week, but after two seasons, the wheel wells are just completely rusted out. I actually tried using that Fluid Film spray underneath my own truck to stop the rust. You ever use that stuff? It works great, but it smells like sheep, literally, because it's made out of lanolin or something. My truck smelled like a petting zoo for weeks. You'd park in the sun and the whole cab would just reek of it. 

Anyway... wait, what were you asking? Two months of something? Oh, right, feeling better. Yeah, no. No breaks like that. Just the same dragging feeling, whether it's summer or winter.

inference.note: The patient has described a persistent low mood lasting more than three years without any significant periods of remission lasting two months or more, which supports a diagnosis of persistent depressive disorder (dysthymia). The absence of any substantial improvement over this extended period rules out the possibility of recurrent depressive disorder with episodic course.
